questions.stem: In a grassland ecosystem, grass absorbs 10,000 kJ of energy from the Sun. Grasshoppers that eat the grass obtain 1,000 kJ, and birds that eat the grasshoppers obtain 100 kJ. What percentage of energy is transferred from grasshoppers to birds?
questions.explanation: Energy transfer efficiency = (energy at next level / energy at current level) x 100. From grasshoppers (1,000 kJ) to birds (100 kJ): (100/1000) x 100 = 10%. Typically only about 10% of energy is transferred between trophic levels. The other 90% is lost through respiration, heat, movement, and in waste materials (faeces and urine).

questions.stem: A pyramid of biomass for an ecosystem shows progressively smaller bars from producers to tertiary consumers. Why does biomass decrease at each trophic level?

options.text: There are fewer species at higher trophic levels
Energy is lost through respiration, heat, and waste at each level, so less energy is available to build biomass at the next level
Predators are always smaller than their prey
Producers contain more water than consumers

questions.explanation: At each trophic level, organisms use most of the energy they consume for life processes (respiration releases energy as heat, movement uses energy, and some material is lost as waste). Only about 10% of the energy is converted into new biomass that is available to the next trophic level. This progressive energy loss explains why pyramids of biomass narrow at each level.

questions.stem: Food chains rarely have more than four or five trophic levels. Using your knowledge of energy transfer, explain why.

options.text: There are not enough different species to fill more levels
By the fourth or fifth level, so little energy remains (due to ~90% loss at each transfer) that it cannot support another trophic level
Top predators refuse to eat other predators
The Sun does not provide enough energy for more than five levels

questions.explanation: With approximately 10% energy transfer efficiency at each level, if producers have 10,000 kJ, primary consumers get ~1,000 kJ, secondary ~100 kJ, tertiary ~10 kJ, and quaternary ~1 kJ. By the fifth level, there is insufficient energy to sustain a viable population. This thermodynamic constraint limits the number of trophic levels in any food chain.

questions.stem: A farmer wants to maximise the efficiency of energy transfer in food production. Which strategy would be most efficient in terms of energy use?

options.text: Feeding grain to cattle, then eating the beef
Eating the grain directly, cutting out the intermediate trophic level
Feeding grain to cattle, feeding cattle to pigs, then eating the pork

questions.explanation: Eating grain directly means humans are primary consumers (one energy transfer step with ~10% loss). Feeding grain to cattle first means two transfer steps (grain to cattle, cattle to humans), losing ~90% at each step. Eating grain directly is roughly 10 times more energy-efficient. This is why plant-based diets can feed more people from the same area of farmland.

questions.stem: Not all the light energy that falls on a leaf is used in photosynthesis. Which of the following explains why plants only capture a small percentage of incoming solar energy?

options.text: Plants are too small to absorb all the sunlight
Some light is the wrong wavelength (reflected or transmitted), some misses the leaves, and photosynthesis is not 100% efficient at converting absorbed light into chemical energy
Most sunlight is absorbed by the soil before it reaches the plants
Plants only photosynthesize at night when there is no sunlight

questions.explanation: Plants typically capture only 1-3% of incoming solar energy. This is because: not all light hits leaves (some hits the ground, water, etc.), green light is reflected (which is why leaves look green), some light is transmitted through leaves, and the biochemical reactions of photosynthesis are not 100% efficient. This low initial capture rate limits the total energy available to the entire ecosystem.
